title: IndiGo Tightens Grip on Indian Skies as Air India Loses Ground
excerpt: India's largest carrier now commands nearly 65% of the domestic market while Air India's capacity shrinks by double digits, widening the gap between the two rivals amid soaring fuel costs and geopolitical headwinds.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • IndiGo's market share reached 64.9%, while Air India's dropped to 25.6%.
  • Air India reduced domestic capacity by 22% and international by 27%.
  • Total airline capacity in India fell 4.7% year-on-year in July 2026.

  • IndiGo held a 64.9% domestic market share in May 2026, up from around 61% in FY25, while the Air India group slipped to 25.6%.
  • Air India has cut domestic capacity by 22% and international capacity by 27% for the June–August period; IndiGo's domestic cuts are a more modest 5–7%.
  • Total Indian airline capacity in July 2026 is 22.5 million seats, down 4.7% year-on-year, according to OAG data.

IndiGo's dominance of Indian aviation is no longer just a lead — it is becoming a structural advantage that its closest rival appears unable to close. Data released by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation and aviation analytics firm OAG paint a picture of a market where the Gurugram-based low-cost carrier is pulling further ahead, even as the broader industry contracts under the pressure of elevated jet fuel prices and the fallout from the US-Iran conflict.

The Numbers Tell the Story

DGCA figures for May 2026 show IndiGo carrying 99.91 lakh domestic passengers, translating to a 64.9% market share — its highest in years. The Air India group, which includes Air India and its budget arm Air India Express, managed 39.33 lakh passengers for a combined 25.6% share. Akasa Air, the Rakesh Jhunjhunwala-founded upstart, held 5.8% with 8.90 lakh passengers, according to Ministry of Civil Aviation data.

OAG's July 2026 capacity data reinforces the trend. IndiGo is scheduled to operate 11.58 million seats during the month — 51% of India's total market — while Air India trails at 2.77 million seats, a 12% share. Air India's year-on-year capacity has cratered by 19.2%, and Air India Express has dropped 16.8%. Meanwhile, Akasa Air grew its seats by 7.4%, the fastest rate among the top ten carriers.

"IndiGo's international platform today is substantially larger and more diversified than it was a year ago."

— Jainam Shah, Aviation Analyst, Equirus Securities

Why Air India Is Shrinking

The Tata Group-owned carrier is fighting fires on multiple fronts. Air India has trimmed domestic frequencies by 22% for the June–August window and cut international capacity by 27% across 33 routes in four regions, according to Airways Magazine. The airline is expected to report nearly $3 billion in losses for FY26, driven by soaring operating costs from the West Asia conflict, which has forced westbound flights to bypass Pakistani airspace on longer, more expensive routings.

"In continuation of our previously announced adjustments to select international services between June and August 2026, we have temporarily rationalized operations on certain domestic routes during the same period, with a reduction in frequencies on select routes," Air India said in a statement.

In contrast, IndiGo's domestic cuts amount to just 5–7%, and the carrier reported a comparatively modest loss of ₹2,394 crore for FY26. Its international network, while affected, has proven more resilient — IndiGo led Air India on international routes in three of the first four months of 2026, according to Livemint.

Broader Market Under Pressure

India's total airline capacity in July 2026 stands at 22.5 million seats, down 4.7% from a year ago, according to OAG. Domestic capacity fell 4.6% to 14.9 million seats, while international capacity dropped 4.8% to 7.6 million seats. Several key airports saw sharp declines: Hyderabad's domestic capacity shrank 15.6%, Chennai fell 15.5%, and Kolkata dropped 12.5%. Mumbai lost 11.6% of capacity. Delhi, however, grew 6.5% to remain India's busiest airport with 2.60 million seats.

The January-to-May 2026 period saw domestic airlines carry 729.40 lakh passengers, a modest 1.91% year-on-year increase. Load factors remained healthy — Akasa Air led at 92.5%, followed by SpiceJet at 87.4% and IndiGo at 86.4%.

What It Means for Travelers

For the Indian diaspora flying home this summer, the capacity squeeze means fewer options and likely higher fares. Air India's route rationalization affects some of its busiest corridors from Delhi and Mumbai, while IndiGo's cuts are more targeted. The airline has signaled further adjustments could come later in the year, including a temporary suspension of its Manchester route.

"As we enter a seasonally softer demand environment from mid-June onwards, combined with elevated fuel prices, we are adopting a measured approach to optimize capacity."

— Gaurav Negi, CFO, IndiGo

What Comes Next

Both airlines have described the cuts as temporary, contingent on fuel prices and geopolitical conditions stabilizing. IndiGo's management has laid out an ambitious long-term target of growing international available seat kilometers from 28% to 40% of its total by FY30. Air India's path looks harder — its transformation under Tata ownership is now colliding with macro headwinds that have amplified its structural disadvantages, particularly on long-haul routes to North America and Europe. The coming months will test whether this is a temporary setback for Air India or the moment the gap became permanent.
